draft:
Public court records can be public in law and private in practice. If the door is open but the hallway costs hundreds or thousands of dollars, the public has been invited into a room it can't reach. Digital access was supposed to remove the distance between you and the courthouse (the bus ride, the missed shift, the childcare scramble). Instead, expensive databases can turn distance into a tollbooth – and call the toll “convenience.”

Imagine you need a filing to understand why your landlord, employer, or local government is taking action against you. You know the record exists. You may even know its case number. But the useful search sits behind a subscription you can't justify, and each wrong click spends money you needed elsewhere. What exactly is “public” about a system that lets a well-funded repeat player search broadly while telling you to ration curiosity? The answer is ugly: access has been allocated by wallet rather than by right.

Defenders of paid access can make a serious point: digital records cost money to store, index, protect, and deliver. Of course they do. A usable system needs staff, security, redaction, and maintenance (none of which appears by magic). But that concession doesn't settle who should pay, any more than the cost of maintaining a courtroom settles whether only subscribers may hear the judge. Public infrastructure has costs; turning those costs into a gate on individual inspection changes the character of the right.

When I test a rule like this, I start with the person least able to absorb friction. A large firm can treat database fees as overhead; you experience them as a warning to stop looking. That asymmetry matters because court records show state power in motion – a prosecution, a judgment, an eviction, a dispute given official force. If we make observation expensive, we haven't made the courts cheaper; we've made scrutiny selective. The machinery still runs, but only the people with an expense account can see all its gears.

Price also shapes what the public learns. If every exploratory search carries a charge, researchers, reporters, defendants, and neighbors will pursue fewer weak signals – precisely the searches that sometimes reveal a pattern. You can't know in advance which docket will matter; discovery requires room to be wrong. A paywall taxes failed hypotheses, so it favors institutions that can afford ten dead ends for one useful lead (ordinary people get one shot). That isn't neutral administration.

This is where the market analogy becomes a scam. We own the courthouse, pay for the judge, create the record, and then meet a private cashier on the way out. The cashier hasn't created the public event; it has packaged the route to it. Some packaging may deserve payment. A basic path to the underlying record shouldn't. Otherwise we're paying admission to inspect our own institution, which is a damn peculiar definition of ownership.

The remedy doesn't require abolishing private tools. Vendors can sell faster search, alerts, analytics, bulk workflows, and polished interfaces to customers who value them. Public access can coexist with premium service (a map may be free even when a guided tour isn't). The baseline should be a complete, searchable, reasonably current public system with fees limited to genuine exceptional costs. That preserves room for competition without letting a vendor become the bouncer at a civic doorway.

There are hard questions: privacy, sealed material, mistaken identity, and the danger of making old allegations frictionlessly permanent. Those problems deserve careful rules and humane design. They aren't an excuse to sell broad visibility to professionals while giving everyone else a keyhole. I don't want openness confused with indiscriminate exposure; I want the public terms of access set by public obligations. If a record may govern your liberty, home, work, or reputation, you should be able to find it without first proving you can afford the search. Keep the courthouse door digital, but keep it public.
